extracted.intended_audience: industry stakeholders, national member bodies, technical experts, consumer representatives, NGOs, academia and government officials interested in developing or participating in ISO standards
extracted.subtask_description: Official guidance on the ISO standards development process: who proposes and drafts standards, the principles that govern development (market need, expert input, multi‑stakeholder participation, consensus), voting and commenting, and routes for urgent work (IWAs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to a need in the market
rubrics_metrics.description: ISO does not unilaterally decide when to develop a new standard; it responds to a request from industry or other stakeholders (e.g., consumer groups) communicated via the national member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposal for new work normally comes from an industry sector or stakeholder group to its national member, who then contacts ISO. Standards should address an identified market need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developed by independent technical experts nominated by members
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards are created by groups of independent technical experts who are nominated by ISO members; ISO acts as a conductor coordinating their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These experts form technical committees and begin by developing a draft that meets the identified market need. Participation is by nomination from national member bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Based on global expert opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: ISO standards are developed by international groups of experts (technical committees) and reflect negotiated expert views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts negotiate all aspects of a standard, including its scope, key definitions and content. The standard should therefore reflect globally informed technical consensus rather than a single national viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developed through a multi-stakeholder process
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical committees include not only industry experts but also representatives from consumer associations, academia, NGOs and government to ensure multiple perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder diversity is an explicit principle; contributions from different sectors are expected and help shape scope, definitions, and content. See 'who develops ISO standards' for membership detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Based on a consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: ISO follows a consensus-based approach where comments from all stakeholders are taken into account during development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The voting process is central: a draft is circulated, stakeholders comment and discuss, and a vote determines whether consensus has been achieved. If consensus is not reached the draft is revised and voted on again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting, commenting and iterative modification
rubrics_metrics.description: The process begins with a draft that addresses the market need, which is then shared for commenting and further discussion; drafts are modified in response to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public or stakeholder commenting rounds and technical meetings feed into revisions. Iteration continues until consensus through voting is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting process as the key to approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval of a draft standard depends on formal voting to demonstrate consensus among members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If agreement is achieved in voting the draft advances toward publication. If agreement is not achieved the draft is revised and re-submitted to vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of International Workshop Agreements (IWAs) for urgent market needs
rubrics_metrics.description: For urgent market needs, ISO provides a route via International Workshop Agreements (IWAs) to address work more rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on new work documents introduce the IWA concept and explain how to propose committees or IWAs when speed is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical timeline from proposal to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: From first proposal to final publication, developing an ISO standard usually takes about three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an approximate timeline; the process includes multiple meetings, commenting rounds and voting steps. Around 26 technical meetings take place globally on a typical working day, reflecting ongoing international activity.
